doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Improvisation within a framework
summary: Armstrong's solos were worked out with endless variation, as with Coltrane; early New Orleans bands had few soloists.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you suppose that performance, and especially that introduction was completely spontaneous?

No I don’t think so. I never talked to Louis about that, but I’m sure — man as I get older I get hoarser talking, talking — I’m sure that he had a pattern worked out, just as you can hear in the many, many performances of things that he did constantly in performances, broadcasts and so forth. The British trumpet player Humphrey Lyttelton wrote a very good piece many years ago about the people who say oh he just plays the same solo over and over again. And he pointed out that he certainly does not and he cited examples on records and he said the pattern was worked out but within it, the variation is endless. And that’s very true of all musicians really. If you study even let’s say someone like John Coltrane, who was a very spontaneous performer, he had things worked out, just as all musicians have, because jazz isn’t simply spontaneous improvisation, it’s improvisation within a framework. And the framework is very important when you have an ensemble going. The early New Orleans bands had no soloists to speak of in their performances. Occasionally there would be a clarinet solo, and I always thought it was to relieve the pressure on the brass players because New Orleans jazz really grew more out of the parade, outdoors music than anything else. And that was a heavy burden for those guys blowing those instruments and blowing them hard for hours on end.
